description: Charlotte boiler, header and power-piping shops: Level III preparation of the NDE side of an ASME S, PP, A, U or R review. Request a gap assessment today.
h1: ASME Certificate Audit Support in Charlotte, North Carolina: NDE Readiness for Power-Sector Code Shops
html:
Charlotte's Code shops mostly build for the power sector: boiler parts, headers, feedwater heaters, boiler external piping and the vessels that sit around a generating unit. If your shop holds an S, PP, A or U designator, or a National Board R certificate, and a review is on the calendar, Atlantis NDT can prepare the nondestructive examination portion of your quality control system. We are an ASNT NDT Level III consulting company, and we work on the written practice, the Section V procedures, examiner certification files, outside-lab controls and the records your Authorized Inspector signs against. Send us your designators and review date; we reply within one business day.

A city built around electricity

Few American cities are as tied to one industry's engineering as Charlotte is to power generation. The investor-owned utility headquartered in the city operates coal, natural gas, hydroelectric and nuclear stations across North and South Carolina, and an engineering and supply chain has grown up around that fleet: design firms, outage contractors, valve and pump service shops, heat exchanger re-tubers, and fabricators who make the pressure parts a unit needs during an outage. Around them sit the region's other steam users, from food and beverage plants to the boilers that still run in mills across the Piedmont.

For a pressure-equipment shop that mix means a heavy share of ASME Section I and B31.1 work. Typical jobs include superheater and reheater tube assemblies, header repairs, attemperators, drains and blowdown piping, boiler external piping, and replacement components for heat recovery steam generators behind combined-cycle gas turbines. Section VIII work shows up as deaerators, feedwater heaters, air receivers, blowdown tanks and the hydropneumatic tanks that water systems across the state rely on. A smaller group of shops installs and assembles boilers in the field, which brings the A and S designators into play.

Nuclear work in the region, and where Atlantis stops

Charlotte also has a deep pool of nuclear engineering talent, and some fabricators in the area hold certificates for nuclear construction alongside their conventional ones. Atlantis does not take on nuclear quality assurance in any form. We do not support Section III fabrication, N-type certificates, NQA-1 programs or 10 CFR 50 quality requirements, and we will not edit a quality manual that governs nuclear work. If your shop runs separate nuclear and non-nuclear programs, we confine ourselves to the non-nuclear manual and the S, PP, A, U or R scope it covers. Saying this at the start saves you from discovering it halfway through a review.

The North Carolina Boiler Safety Bureau

Boilers and pressure vessels in North Carolina fall under Chapter 95, Article 7A of the General Statutes, enforced by the Boiler Safety Bureau of the North Carolina Department of Labor. The bureau's rules matter to a stamp shop in several concrete ways:

  • Current Code, every section. The National Board's synopsis of state laws shows North Carolina adopting the current edition of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and the National Board Inspection Code (Parts 2, 3 and 4). There is no older edition to fall back on when your manual lags.
  • Registration. Boilers and pressure vessels must be registered with the National Board, and manufacturers file their Manufacturer's Data Reports on the ASME forms with the National Board. The NDE summary on that report has to be supported by examination records you can produce.
  • Repairs. The NBIC is mandatory for repairs and alterations, welded repairs must be done by an R certificate holder, and the holder files its Form R report with the chief inspector after the work is complete, by a deadline set in the rules.
  • Installations. The bureau notes that some power boiler installations require the installer to hold an ASME Certificate of Authorization, and a North Carolina-commissioned inspector inspects equipment when it is installed.
  • Owner-user programs. Companies that inspect their own pressure vessels need commissioned owner-user inspectors who pass an examination on North Carolina law, under a program supervised by qualified engineers.
  • In-service intervals. High-pressure boilers are inspected internally and externally each year, pressure vessels externally every two years and hydropneumatic tanks every four years, and nothing covered by the law may operate without a current inspection certificate.

Confirm the edition in force and any recent changes with the bureau before you lock your manual revision. The rules apply to equipment installed in North Carolina; if you ship into South Carolina, Virginia or Tennessee, that state's chief inspector applies its own rules at the installation.

The NDE profile of a power-sector Code shop

Section I work leans on different examinations than a general vessel shop sees. Expect the review team and your Authorized Inspector to look closely at:

  • Volumetric examination of butt welds. Section I's volumetric rules (paragraph PW-11) set when circumferential and longitudinal butt welds in drums, headers and piping need radiography or ultrasonic examination, and on what conditions UT can take the place of RT. Your drawings, travelers and NDE plan should show which rule applied to each weld.
  • Tube-to-header and attachment welds. These usually get visual examination plus magnetic particle or penetrant testing to the construction code's acceptance criteria, and they are where an examiner's surface preparation and lighting are most often questioned.
  • Chrome-moly and creep-strength enhanced alloys. Grade 91 and similar steels bring post-weld heat treatment records and, frequently, owner-specified hardness checks. Hardness testing is not a Section V method, but utilities often want it in the same turnover package as the NDE, so your manual should say who does it and how it is recorded.
  • Boiler external piping. Piping from the boiler to the first stop valve falls under Section I's jurisdiction, with B31.1 construction rules and Section I's inspection and stamping requirements, and only holders of the right certificates may build or install it. See our ASME B31.1 summary for the examination rules.
  • Thickness readings. Ultrasonic thickness measurements on tubes and headers taken during repairs feed engineering decisions. When those readings are part of a Code record, they need a written procedure and a calibrated instrument, just like any other examination.

In Section V terms, a power-sector shop's procedure binder normally holds a visual procedure to Article 9, magnetic particle to Article 7, penetrant to Article 6, weld ultrasonics to Article 4, and the radiographic requirements of Article 2 that its outside lab must meet. Our Section I explainer walks through the boiler code itself.

Field crews, outages and the NDE paperwork they generate

Much of the Code work done by Charlotte-area firms happens away from the shop: tube replacements inside a boiler during a spring outage, header repairs in a turbine hall, piping tie-ins at a combined-cycle plant. That is where NDE records most often go astray. The examining company works on its own report forms, examiners rotate between night and day shifts, and the radiographs or data files leave with the crew. When the review comes, the shop is asked to produce records for field jobs on its Code work list and finds them scattered.

A sound field program answers a few questions in writing. Who accepts each outside examiner before that person touches a Code weld? How does the examination record get back into your job file in a form you control? Who in your company reviews outside reports and radiographs before the Authorized Inspector sees them? And when the plant's own inspector or the insurer's inspector asks for the NDE behind an R-form repair, how quickly can someone hand it over? Our subcontractor approval audit method addresses the first question; the rest belongs in your QC manual.

Atlantis holds no radiography license in the United States and does not shoot radiographs here, so radiography on Carolinas jobs stays with a licensed company. As a Level III we can review the images, the technique and the report on your behalf, and help you write the requirements your purchase order places on that company.

How the review team will look at your NDE

ASME's joint review starts with the team reading your quality control manual, then moves to your shop, where it watches the manual in use, either on a live Code job or on a practice piece built only for the review and never stamped. For a power-sector shop the demonstration might be a header section with a few stub welds and a butt weld, or a short run of boiler external piping. The team typically follows each examination from the point the drawing calls for it to the line on the data report that records it, and stops wherever the trail breaks.

At renewal, the list of Code work you submit includes field jobs, so every outage repair is fair game. For bought-in NDE, ASME's guidance expects the subcontractor's procedure and personnel qualification files to be available where the review happens, which means copies in your office, not a promise that the lab can email them.

NDE findings we see in shops with this work mix:

  • PW-11 examinations performed, but the record does not show which weld was examined by which method or why UT was used in place of RT.
  • Field examiners accepted verbally by a superintendent rather than through the process the manual describes.
  • Penetrant consumables from a field kit with no batch record, or a cleaner that is not on the procedure.
  • Ultrasonic thickness gauges used for Code records with no calibration certificate on file.
  • A written practice that names an SNT-TC-1A edition different from the one the QC manual cites.
  • Examiner vision records that lapsed during a busy outage season.

Atlantis's work for Charlotte shops

Atlantis works from offices in Houston and Hyderabad. For Charlotte engagements, document review and drafting are done remotely and site visits are planned around your schedule, often timed to avoid your customers' outage peaks. A typical scope:

  • Gap assessment of the NDE sections of your QC manual against the current Code edition North Carolina enforces and against your utility customers' specifications.
  • Drafting or revising the written practice so it covers in-house examiners, field examiners from outside companies and the acceptance of substitutes.
  • Section V procedures and technique sheets for VT, MT, PT and UT, and the radiographic requirements you place on your lab, through our procedure development work.
  • Preparing for a procedure demonstration where your Authorized Inspector asks to witness one.
  • Auditing certification files: training, experience logs, examinations and vision records, and giving Level III examinations under your written practice. Your company signs every certification.
  • A mock review on your demonstration item and help closing any findings with corrective-action evidence.

Anoop Rayavarapu, Atlantis's founder, takes these engagements personally. He is certified to ASNT NDT Level III in visual, penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic and radiographic testing and has spent more than 11 years on inspection projects internationally. Shops that need their examiners trained before certification can look at NDT training for Charlotte or the power-generation NDT training page.

Who decides, who certifies, who welds

Your company holds the certificate and owns the quality control system; your quality manager speaks for it. Your company certifies its own NDE personnel under its written practice, and our examinations and recommendations support that decision without replacing it. Judging the system is the job of the ASME team and your Authorized Inspection Agency, with the certificate decision made by ASME itself. Atlantis signs no data reports or R forms, acts as no one's Authorized Inspection Agency and certifies nobody.

The welding program, from WPS and PQR to welder and operator qualification under Section IX, sits with the welder-qualification and procedure owner in your company, usually a welding engineer. Atlantis stays out of welding procedure writing and qualification entirely; for background on what reviewers expect there, read the WPS, PQR and WPQ guide.

Charlotte readiness checklist for the NDE portion

  • Your QC manual, written practice and procedures cite one SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition, matching what your Code edition references.
  • The NDE plan for Section I work shows the PW-11 basis for each volumetric examination and the reason UT replaced RT wherever it did.
  • Field examiners are accepted through a written step before they examine Code welds, and the acceptance is recorded.
  • Outside NDE companies each have a file in your office with their written practice, examiner certifications, procedures with your review recorded, and calibration evidence.
  • Radiography subcontractors' radioactive materials licenses are on file, and radiographs for Code jobs are retrievable for the full retention period your manual sets.
  • Field reports from outage work come back into your job files on forms you control.
  • Thickness gauges, yokes, flaw detectors, light meters and reference blocks are on one calibration list with no overdue items in use.
  • Hardness and heat-treatment records required by utility specifications are tied to the same joints as the NDE records.
  • Repair packages under the R certificate show NDE performed to the original code of construction and are ready to accompany the Form R report.
  • Your Code work list for renewal includes every field site, and each listed job has its NDE records.
  • Someone other than the person who wrote the manual has walked the demonstration item from drawing to data report.

If certification and calibration dates are tracked by hand, the pages on expired technician certifications and certificate tracking show how a shop keeps them visible.

Getting started: what to send and how the work proceeds

Send the NDE chapters of the quality control manual, the written practice, the procedure index, three examiner certification files, the files you keep on each NDE subcontractor, your calibration register and one recently completed Section I or B31.1 job package with its data report. For a renewal, add the draft list of Code work, including field jobs.

  1. We confirm scope with a call: designators, Authorized Inspection Agency, review date, and which methods are in house.
  2. We return a written gap report that ranks each gap by how likely a review team is to write it up and cites the Code or practice clause behind it.
  3. We draft revisions for your quality manager to approve; nothing enters your manual without your sign-off.
  4. We visit Charlotte for a mock implementation, a records walkthrough and any Level III examinations you need.
  5. We stay on call around the review and help assemble corrective-action evidence afterwards.

The national ASME audit Level III support page covers the certification process in more depth, and our NBIC R-stamp audit support page covers repair certificates.

faq.q: Does North Carolina send someone to our ASME joint review?
faq.a: That depends on how your review is arranged. The team is led by ASME with your Authorized Inspection Agency, and a jurisdictional or National Board representative may take part. Ask your AIA who will attend from North Carolina well before the date.

faq.q: Our shop builds boiler external piping. Which certificate covers it?
faq.a: Boiler external piping falls under Section I's jurisdiction, so it is built and installed by holders of the applicable ASME certificates rather than as plain B31.1 work. Your AIA can confirm which designator fits your scope. The NDE for that piping must follow the Section I and B31.1 rules your manual cites.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic examination replace radiography on our Section I welds?
faq.a: Section I's volumetric examination rules allow it under defined conditions. Your procedure, examiner qualifications and records must meet those conditions, and the job file should show why UT was chosen for each weld. Our procedure development service covers UT procedures written for this use.

faq.q: Will Atlantis help with the nuclear side of our quality program?
faq.a: No. Section III fabrication, N-type certificates and NQA-1 programs are not part of our work. We support only the non-nuclear certificates and the manual that governs them.

faq.q: Our NDE crews change between outage shifts. How should the manual deal with that?
faq.a: Write a short acceptance step: before any examiner touches a Code weld, an authorized person checks that examiner's certification and methods against your accepted list and records the check. That step is cheap to run and one of the first things a reviewer asks about for field work.

faq.q: Does Atlantis carry out radiography on Charlotte jobs?
faq.a: No. Atlantis takes no radiographs in the United States. A licensed radiography company does that work, and we can review its images, techniques and reports as a Level III.

faq.q: Who signs our examiners' certifications if Atlantis gives the Level III exams?
faq.a: Your company does. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, and an outside Level III can examine and recommend as your written practice allows. Our training records and certificates page shows how the file should look.

faq.q: Do hardness checks on Grade 91 piping belong in the NDE section of the manual?
faq.a: Hardness testing is not a Section V examination, but many utility specifications require it, and reviewers will ask how it is controlled when it appears in your job files. Put it wherever your manual handles owner-required tests, with a named responsible person and a record format.

faq.q: Can Atlantis write our welding procedures for Section I?
faq.a: No. WPS, PQR and welder qualification belong to your welding engineer, and Atlantis neither writes nor qualifies welding procedures.

faq.q: How much of the preparation happens in Charlotte?
faq.a: Document review and drafting are remote. We come to Charlotte for the mock implementation, the records walkthrough with your team and any examinations you want given in person.
